pages.text: In a museum, Mrs Konadu laid a velvet tray in front of Kukua and Kwarteng. On it sat dozens of tiny brass figures: a bird, a fish, a stool, a crocodile, a spiral. “These are Akan goldweights,” she said. “People used them to weigh gold dust, which was long a main form of money in the region.”
sentences: In a museum, Mrs Konadu laid a velvet tray in front of Kukua and Kwarteng.
On it sat dozens of tiny brass figures: a bird, a fish, a stool, a crocodile, a spiral.
“These are Akan goldweights,” she said.
“People used them to weigh gold dust, which was long a main form of money in the region.”
pages.alt: A curator shows a tray of tiny brass figures to two students.

pages.text: “How were they made?” asked Kwarteng. “By the lost-wax method,” said Mrs Konadu. “A model is made from beeswax and covered in clay. The wax is melted out, leaving a hollow. Then molten brass is poured in. When it cools, the clay is broken away.” “So each one is unique,” said Kukua. “Yes. The wax model is destroyed every time.”

pages.text: “Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc,” said Mrs Konadu. “Museum records tell us there are two main kinds of weights. The oldest are geometric: spirals, lines and circles. They are dated to about the fifteenth century. Later came figurative weights, shaped like animals, people and objects, from about the year 1600.” Kukua wrote: abstract first, figures later.

pages.text: Kwarteng took out his small kitchen scale. “How did they weigh?” “With a balance and a set of weights,” said Mrs Konadu. “Some geometric weights follow the Arab unit called the mithqal, about 4.6 grams. Europeans later brought other units, like the ackie. People often added tiny pieces of lead to adjust a weight to the standard.” Kwarteng did a sum: “So three mithqal would weigh about 13.8 grams.”

pages.text: “Now here is where it gets interesting,” said Mrs Konadu. “Many of the figurative pieces may not have been weights at all. Some historians think they were objects that carried proverbs, rules and judgments. A crocodile with two heads and one stomach, for example, might remind people that we share one stomach, so we should work together.” Kukua grinned. “A proverb you can hold!”

pages.text: “And the geometric ones?” asked Kukua. “That is the mystery,” said Mrs Konadu. “Many of their patterns look like adinkra stamps and the decorations on shrines, and may link to proverbs. But the meaning of most of the geometric designs is unknown. Some may have marked specific weights. Perhaps some patterns were a kind of code.”

pages.text: Kukua studied a spiral through her magnifying glass. “How could we find out what the patterns mean?” “By comparing many weights, by collecting oral history from families who kept them, by studying records from traders, and by asking whether the same pattern always matches the same weight,” said Mrs Konadu. “Every new clue helps.”

“How could we find out what the patterns mean?” “By comparing many weights, by collecting oral history from families who kept them, by studying records from traders, and by asking whether the same pattern always matches the same weight,” said Mrs Konadu.
“Every new clue helps.”
pages.alt: A girl with a magnifying glass studies a spiral weight.

pages.text: At the end, Kwarteng and Kukua made a list. Known: the weights were cast in brass and used in trade. Debated: whether the figures were weights, proverbs or both. Unknown: what most geometric patterns mean. “So the weights are small,” said Kwarteng, “but the questions are big.” Mrs Konadu smiled. “That,” she said, “is why we keep them safe.” The end.
